title: Time Based Key-Value Store
summary: Design a class `TimeMap` that keeps every value a key has ever had. `set(key, value, timestamp)` records that `key` held `value` from that moment on. `get(key, timestamp)` returns the value the key held at `timestamp`: the one stored with the largest timestamp at or before it, or an empty string if the key had no value yet. Timestamps passed to `set` only ever increase.

examples.input: set("lamp", "off", 2), set("lamp", "on", 7), get("lamp", 1), get("lamp", 5), get("lamp", 7), get("lamp", 30)
examples.explanation: At time 1 the lamp had no value yet. From time 2 it was "off", and from time 7 on it is "on".
Each key has its own history; "c" was never set.

constraints: Timestamps passed to set only ever increase
At most 2·10⁵ calls to set and get in total

approaches.twist: Append (timestamp, value) pairs to a list per key, already sorted, and binary search for the last timestamp ≤ the query.
Keep each key's (timestamp, value) list and scan it backward for the first timestamp at or before the query.
approaches.note: Works, but a key with a long history makes each get O(n). The history is already sorted, so binary search makes get O(log n).

signals.meaning: Appending each new (timestamp, value) to the key's list keeps the list sorted for free, so a get can binary search it.

signals.phrase: the largest timestamp at or before it
signals.meaning: Find the last position whose timestamp is ≤ the query: binary search for the first timestamp that is too late, then step back one.

signals.phrase: every value a key has ever had
signals.meaning: One dict from key to that key's history: a list of (timestamp, value) pairs.

constraintReading: Up to 2·10⁵ calls. If one key gets 10⁵ sets, scanning its history on each of 10⁵ gets is about 10¹⁰ steps: O(n) per get is too slow. The history is sorted by timestamp because timestamps only increase, so each get can be an O(log n) binary search. Every value is kept: O(n) space.

hints.clarify: What does a get between two sets return? The older value: after set("k", "a", 10) and set("k", "b", 20), get("k", 15) is "a", get("k", 20) is "b", and get("k", 5) is "" because nothing was set yet. Can a later set use a smaller timestamp? No, timestamps only increase.
hints.approach: Hash map from key to its history, plus binary search. `set` appends (timestamp, value) to the key's list; since timestamps only increase, the list stays sorted by timestamp. `get` binary searches that list for the last entry whose timestamp is ≤ the query: when the middle entry is at or before the query, remember its value and look further right; when it's too late, look left. The last value remembered is the answer, or "" if none was.
hints.whyNot: Scanning a key's history backward on every get is O(n) per call when one key has many values. Storing the value for every timestamp from 1 to 10⁷ uses far too much memory. Sorting the history on every get wastes the order that the increasing timestamps already give you.

slots.setup: A dict from each key to a list of (timestamp, value) pairs, in the order they were set. For a get, `lo` = 0 and `hi` = the last index of that key's list, and an answer of "".
slots.update: If the middle entry's timestamp is ≤ the query, move `lo` to mid + 1 to look for a later one that also fits; otherwise move `hi` to mid − 1.
slots.record: Each time the middle entry fits (timestamp ≤ query), save its value as the best answer so far.
slots.return: Return the saved value, or "" when no entry fit or the key was never set.

solution.explanation: `set` appends to a list: O(1). `get` halves the key's history at every step: O(log n) for a key with n entries. Every (timestamp, value) pair is kept: O(n) space for n sets. `self.store.get(key, [])` reads a missing key without adding it to the defaultdict, so gets never grow the store. `bisect_right(entries, (timestamp, chr(0x10FFFF)))` would find the same position in one line.

events.label: set
events.say: Append ({timestamp}, {value!r}) to the history of {key!r}. Timestamps only increase, so the history stays sorted

events.label: check
events.say: get({key!r}, {timestamp}): the middle entry of {lo}..{hi} was set at time {entries[mid][0]}

events.label: fits
events.say: {entries[mid][0]} ≤ {timestamp}, so {entries[mid][1]!r} is a candidate. A later entry may fit too: look right

events.label: too late
events.say: {entries[mid][0]} is after {timestamp}, so this entry and everything after it are too late: look left

events.label: return
events.say: The range is empty. The latest entry at or before {timestamp} gives {ans!r}

predict.ask: Does this entry come at or before the asked time?
Does this entry come at or before the asked time?

related.relation: The same search for a boundary in a sorted list: there the first position ≥ the target, here the last timestamp ≤ the query.
Also a design problem where each call must be fast, so the work is done when values are stored, not when they're asked for.
